# Lessons of glibc-crustify

Rules that hold for this campaign alone, as `evolution`'s Lessons section describes. Every
run reads them before its first step.

## A batch's gates run with no build variant

**Rule.** libc is the system's, so `build.json` has no variants, and this tree has no
`cargo-variant` script. A batch runs its gates directly, each build in a target dir of its
own under `crustify/tmp/`:

- campaign mode: `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=<plain | asan-ubsan | tsan>` set on every
  `cargo` command that builds the tests, which then regenerate the bindings and check them
  against the committed ones;
- format: `cargo +<the workspace's nightly> fmt --all -- --check`, since `rustfmt.toml`
  uses nightly-only options;
- ASan: on that nightly, `--target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, with
  `RUSTFLAGS="-Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"`; TSan: the same with
  `-Zsanitizer=thread` and `-Zbuild-std`. They instrument the Rust alone, since the
  system's glibc is not instrumented, so TSan sees no race inside glibc;
- coverage: Rust only, measured as the parent's `crustify/scripts/coverage/baseline.sh`
  does, over a scratch copy without `c/`. Its `report.py` rejects the scope, since
  `llvm-cov` prints this tree's file names relative to `src/`, so the `TOTAL` line is read
  from `llvm-cov report` itself. The compile-fail suite fails in the marked copy, which
  only a nightly builds, and it covers nothing.

**Evidence.** wave-2/batch-0/run-1 (`libio/genops.c`) worked these out by hand.

**Scope.** Every batch until the tree gets a variant script.

---
name: reviewing
description: "How landed work is reviewed: tiered review batches and module passes, depth by how long code lasts, worklists, objectives, reports, reproducers, fixes, gates and plan corrections. Read before reviewing a batch, filing a finding or correcting an earlier plan."
---

# Reviewing

Review inspects work that has already landed, for a set of objectives, and files a report
for every defect it finds. In a translation campaign, it inspects what each
translation batch landed before the waves that build on it start; in an audit, the modules of a crate
that Crustify did not generate (see [`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)); and planner runs review the
plan that earlier runs committed (see [Plan corrections](#9-plan-corrections)).

## 1. Review batches

When review is enabled, every translation batch's landing is reviewed before its wave is
promoted, so that no wave builds on unreviewed work. A review batch is a batch of the wave
it reviews, in `schedule.json`, that `reviews` some of its landed translation batches, and
lands on the same integration branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)
names it. The wave is promoted
once its translation batches and their reviews have landed. An audit's review waves are
[`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)'s.

Review is tiered. Each landing is reviewed within its wave, to the depth
[Depth](#11-depth) gives it. Before a module's switch in a port, and at its end in a
wrap, a module pass reviews the module whole, across its batches: its unsafe regions, its
exports and its tests. It is the last review batch of the last wave of the module's `wrap`
and `port` items, not of a port's later stages, marked
`module_pass`, launched once every other batch of that wave has landed; its worklist is
the module's paths, and it runs the wave's gates and the module's end gates, as
[Gates](#7-gates) describes. A module whose run landed a single translation batch is
reviewed by its module pass alone, whose workset is that batch's whole: a review of the
batch before it would read the same code twice.

Review batches are packed eagerly, as the batches they review land: one launches as soon as
the landed batches not yet reviewed fill it, and the last once every translation batch of
the wave has landed, so that review runs beside the wave's remaining batches rather than
after them. When a session runs only part of a wave, or part of the scope, its review
covers what it landed, before what consumes that starts.

A review batch takes the commits of translation batches of one route, `type` or `symbol`,
counted over their items: types and symbols are reviewed apart. It is larger than a
translation batch, since its reviewer reads landed code rather than writing it, and is
sized as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Batches section sizes one,
from what landed rather than what is planned: its lines, its unsafe sites and raw-pointer
positions, the regions it touches and the objectives it carries, without overwhelming its
reviewer, and within the settings' review caps (`id: review-workload`) when they set them.
A campaign may also review every translation batch on its own, with that batch's commits.

A review batch's `task.json` holds its worklist, its objectives, its wave branch and its
run fields, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Review batches section
describes. Without `objectives`, a batch runs every objective that applies: those this skill's
Objectives section and the tool skills describe.

### 1.1 Depth

How deeply a landing is reviewed follows how long its code lasts, as
[`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)'s thoroughness does. A wrapper a port will replace, its
item's port planned in `schedule.json`, keeps its safe API through that port: it is
reviewed on its public API, for every objective that applies there, `ergonomics` included,
and not on its internals. An export is reviewed lightly while the C that calls it is
scheduled for porting, and thoroughly once it serves C that stays, for good or when a ship
point releases its module. Everything else is reviewed for every objective that applies.

## 2. Worklists

A review batch has one route:

| route | worklist | workset |
|---|---|---|
| `commits` | commits that translation batches landed | the code they add or change, and what it reaches |
| `paths` | source files and directories of a crate, or named types, trait impls and functions in one | everything they define, or the named parts |
| `reports` | none: the batch only revisits reports | the code the reports name |

A review batch's entry in `schedule.json` names the batches of its wave it
`reviews`, and each of those lists the `commits` it landed and the `items` it bound or
ported, whose `kind` gives their routes, `type` or `symbol`, as
[`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section describes.

A module named with `types`, `trait_impls` or `functions` limits the workset to those: a
type with its fields and its inherent impls, wherever they are; a trait impl, named
`<trait> for <type>` as its header spells it, with its methods and associated items; a
free function with nothing else. What they call and what implements their traits is read,
but only the workset is reported on.

## 3. Objectives

Each objective names a kind of defect. A tool may contribute objectives of its own.

### 3.1 Unsafety (`unsafety`)

Unsafe annotations and raw pointers on the workset's public API that safe, idiomatic
variants could replace, so that API consumers write less unsafe code.

### 3.2 Contracts (`contracts`)

Safety contracts that are incorrect, incomplete or ambiguous:

- the `# Safety` obligation of a public entry point that must legitimately stay unsafe: a
  caller who honours it can still reach undefined behaviour, or it asks for something the
  implementation does not need;
- the `// SAFETY:` justification of an `unsafe` block: the invariant it claims does not
  hold on every path that reaches the block, or no comment justifies the block at all;
- an obligation stated on code that C calls once a value is handed to it, such as the
  members of a callback table a safe constructor builds for C to install: C, not the Rust
  caller, then chooses the arguments, often from data it reads, so no caller can honour it.
  What the obligation excludes is refused in Rust, in front of the C, instead, where Rust
  can test it, such as a value, a range, a null or a length. One Rust cannot test, such as
  a pointer's liveness or family, or a string's terminator, is kept by whoever hands the
  value to C: the C declaration's own contract, which the code it calls trusts as an
  export does, or an `unsafe` installer whose Rust caller vouches for it. Only an
  obligation neither covers, and Rust can test, is a finding.

A contract is tested by trying to break it: an input, a call sequence or an interleaving
that honours the obligation, or reaches the block through safe code, and still violates
what the `unsafe` relies on. Contracts are judged by the side of the boundary they serve:
the gateways through which C reaches the crate, its `ffi_export` regions, and every other
unsafe code, which in a Crustify-generated crate sits in its `ffi_import` regions, whose
items are sound for every input their module can give them, as
[`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section requires.

### 3.3 UB (`ub`)

UB in the workset's API that its UB tests missed, by where it is reached from: the safe
public API, the unsafe public API within its `# Safety` obligations, or C through an
export within the C declaration's contract. The unsafe surface includes only the API the
workset adds; a workset that made no API item unsafe has none.

### 3.4 Equivalence (`equiv`)

Functional equivalence defects in the workset's API that its equivalence tests missed,
while the C it translates exists: in a port, until the module's switch. A divergence is a defect only when it is unintended: a doc comment, a `CHANGELOG`
entry, a named test asserting the new behaviour or a commit message explaining it marks it
deliberate, and one that corrects a C defect on purpose is no finding.

### 3.5 Logic (`logic`)

Behaviour that departs from the library's intended specification, in the workset's public
API or its private implementation, that its tests missed. The specification is, from the
most authoritative: the formats and standards the library implements, its documentation,
what its own test suites assert, and its maintainers' stated intent. A finding cites what
the behaviour departs from. Where the C departs from it too, the defect is not copied into
the Rust, and the finding records the C's. A leak, a deadlock or a panic on valid input
departs from nearly every specification.

### 3.6 Ergonomics (`ergonomics`)

Public API that is harder to use than it needs to be: its names, its conversions, its
iterators, builders or defaults where the C takes long argument lists, and the standard
traits its types lack. An item's safe API is fixed by the first batch that gives it one, a
wrap included, so its ergonomics are reviewed there.

### 3.7 Idiom (`idiom`)

Ported implementation that transliterates its C rather than using Rust's own means: index
loops where iterators fit, status codes where `Result` and `?` fit, lengths and releases
carried by hand where ownership carries them.

### 3.8 Conventions (`conventions`)

Deviations from the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md), in a Crustify-generated
batch only, unsafe code outside its regions included.

### 3.9 Misc (`misc`)

Any other defect in the workset.

### 3.10 Test adequacy (`test-adequacy`)

Gaps in the workset's tests: the C and Rust execution paths, and the states and
transitions, that the codebase's external and inline test suites leave unreached, found by
reading those suites against the code and measured as
[`testing-builds`](../testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section describes; assertions too
weak to fail when the code is wrong; tests outside the suite of their kind; and the C test
cases none carries over. A gap is filled with tests, not filed: the coverage measurement
shows the delta.

### 3.11 Revisit (`revisit`)

The reports an earlier review filed, each rerun through its reproducer on the current
tree. One that still reproduces stays a finding of its objective; one that no longer does
has its report updated with the commit that changed the verdict; one that was never a
defect is removed, with the reason in the commit message.

### 3.12 Disclosure (`disclose`)

A `disclosure.md` beside each report that the user can send to the affected project's
maintainers unchanged: under 450 words, following the project's conventions for
disclosing security and UB issues, in an email-friendly format naming the maintainers when
it goes by email first. It includes a small snippet and the sanitizer crash or failing
assertion, offers the reproducer on request, and offers patches only under `fix`. It ends
with: `Found by [Crustify](https://github.com/crustify-rs/crustify), an experimental
UB/soundness auditing agent developed at UC Berkeley and running on <model name>, then
manually reviewed and independently reproduced.`

### 3.13 Fix (`fix`)

Whether a review patches what it finds. Without it, a review changes nothing outside
its reviews dir but the tests that fill the gaps `test-adequacy` finds.

## 4. Reports

A review batch files its findings under its reviews dir, as
[`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Reviews section spells it,
each in its own `<slug>` directory, holding its report and, when it has one, its
reproducer, in the sub-directory of its objective:

| objective | sub-directory |
|---|---|
| `unsafety` | `unsafe/` |
| `contracts`, of a gateway | `contracts/ffi_export/` |
| `contracts`, of other unsafe code | `contracts/ffi_import/` |
| `ub`, on the safe interface | `ub_safe/` |
| `ub`, on the unsafe interface | `ub_unsafe/` |
| `ub`, through an export | `ub_export/` |
| `equiv` | `equiv/` |
| `logic` | `logic/` |
| `ergonomics` | `ergonomics/` |
| `idiom` | `idiom/` |
| `conventions` | `conventions/` |
| `misc` | `misc/` |

A tool may add sub-directories for findings on its own output. A defect in a tool
rather than in the reviewed codebase, Crustify included, is no finding: it is a proposal,
with its reproducer, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)'s Proposals
section describes.

A report states what is wrong, where, the evidence that proves it, and, under `fix`, how
it was fixed. It carries everything needed to rerun its reproducer from a clean checkout:
the exact command and the sanitizer output or failing assertion it produced. Neither a
report nor a reproducer carries an API key, in a core dump or anywhere else: a reviews dir
may be published.

## 5. Reproducers

A `ub`, `equiv` or `logic` candidate becomes a finding only once a reproducer proves it,
and so does a `contracts` candidate that claims a contract can be broken. A contract that merely
asks for more than the implementation needs, or a missing justification, is a finding
without one.

- A UB reproducer triggers one of the available sanitizers from Rust, and its report
  carries the sanitizer's trace. One targeting the safe public API carries

  comparisons while running the raw C and the public Rust API, and its report carries the
  failing assertion. Once the C is gone, a behaviour finding is a `logic` one.

  and its report carries the failing assertion.

description: "How landed work is reviewed: tiered review batches and module passes, depth by how long code lasts, worklists, objectives, reports, reproducers, fixes, gates and plan corrections. Read before reviewing a batch, filing a finding or correcting an earlier plan."

# Reviewing

Review inspects work that has already landed, for a set of objectives, and files a report
for every defect it finds. In a translation campaign, it inspects what each
translation batch landed before the waves that build on it start; in an audit, the modules of a crate
that Crustify did not generate (see [`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)); and planner runs review the
plan that earlier runs committed (see [Plan corrections](#9-plan-corrections)).

## 1. Review batches

When review is enabled, every translation batch's landing is reviewed before its wave is
promoted, so that no wave builds on unreviewed work. A review batch is a batch of the wave
it reviews, in `schedule.json`, that `reviews` some of its landed translation batches, and
lands on the same integration branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)
names it. The wave is promoted
once its translation batches and their reviews have landed. An audit's review waves are
[`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)'s.

Review is tiered. Each landing is reviewed within its wave, to the depth
[Depth](#11-depth) gives it. Before a module's switch in a port, and at its end in a
wrap, a module pass reviews the module whole, across its batches: its unsafe regions, its
exports and its tests. It is the last review batch of the last wave of the module's `wrap`
and `port` items, not of a port's later stages, marked
`module_pass`, launched once every other batch of that wave has landed; its worklist is
the module's paths, and it runs the wave's gates and the module's end gates, as
[Gates](#7-gates) describes. A module whose run landed a single translation batch is
reviewed by its module pass alone, whose workset is that batch's whole: a review of the
batch before it would read the same code twice.

Review batches are packed eagerly, as the batches they review land: one launches as soon as
the landed batches not yet reviewed fill it, and the last once every translation batch of
the wave has landed, so that review runs beside the wave's remaining batches rather than
after them. When a session runs only part of a wave, or part of the scope, its review
covers what it landed, before what consumes that starts.

A review batch takes the commits of translation batches of one route, `type` or `symbol`,
counted over their items: types and symbols are reviewed apart. It is larger than a
translation batch, since its reviewer reads landed code rather than writing it, and is
sized as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Batches section sizes one,
from what landed rather than what is planned: its lines, its unsafe sites and raw-pointer
positions, the regions it touches and the objectives it carries, without overwhelming its
reviewer, and within the settings' review caps (`id: review-workload`) when they set them.
A campaign may also review every translation batch on its own, with that batch's commits.

A review batch's `task.json` holds its worklist, its objectives, its wave branch and its
run fields, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Review batches section
describes. Without `objectives`, a batch runs every objective that applies: those this skill's
Objectives section and the tool skills describe.

### 1.1 Depth

How deeply a landing is reviewed follows how long its code lasts, as
[`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)'s thoroughness does. A wrapper a port will replace, its
item's port planned in `schedule.json`, keeps its safe API through that port: it is
reviewed on its public API, for every objective that applies there, `ergonomics` included,
and not on its internals. An export is reviewed lightly while the C that calls it is
scheduled for porting, and thoroughly once it serves C that stays, for good or when a ship
point releases its module. Everything else is reviewed for every objective that applies.

## 2. Worklists

A review batch has one route:

| route | worklist | workset |
|---|---|---|
| `commits` | commits that translation batches landed | the code they add or change, and what it reaches |
| `paths` | source files and directories of a crate, or named types, trait impls and functions in one | everything they define, or the named parts |
| `reports` | none: the batch only revisits reports | the code the reports name |

A review batch's entry in `schedule.json` names the batches of its wave it
`reviews`, and each of those lists the `commits` it landed and the `items` it bound or
ported, whose `kind` gives their routes, `type` or `symbol`, as
[`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section describes.

A module named with `types`, `trait_impls` or `functions` limits the workset to those: a
type with its fields and its inherent impls, wherever they are; a trait impl, named
`<trait> for <type>` as its header spells it, with its methods and associated items; a
free function with nothing else. What they call and what implements their traits is read,
but only the workset is reported on.

## 3. Objectives

Each objective names a kind of defect. A tool may contribute objectives of its own.

### 3.1 Unsafety (`unsafety`)

Unsafe annotations and raw pointers on the workset's public API that safe, idiomatic
variants could replace, so that API consumers write less unsafe code.

### 3.2 Contracts (`contracts`)

Safety contracts that are incorrect, incomplete or ambiguous:

- the `# Safety` obligation of a public entry point that must legitimately stay unsafe: a
  caller who honours it can still reach undefined behaviour, or it asks for something the
  implementation does not need;
- the `// SAFETY:` justification of an `unsafe` block: the invariant it claims does not
  hold on every path that reaches the block, or no comment justifies the block at all;
- an obligation stated on code that C calls once a value is handed to it, such as the
  members of a callback table a safe constructor builds for C to install: C, not the Rust
  caller, then chooses the arguments, often from data it reads, so no caller can honour it.
  What the obligation excludes is refused in Rust, in front of the C, instead, where Rust
  can test it, such as a value, a range, a null or a length. One Rust cannot test, such as
  a pointer's liveness or family, or a string's terminator, is kept by whoever hands the
  value to C: the C declaration's own contract, which the code it calls trusts as an
  export does, or an `unsafe` installer whose Rust caller vouches for it. Only an
  obligation neither covers, and Rust can test, is a finding.

A contract is tested by trying to break it: an input, a call sequence or an interleaving
that honours the obligation, or reaches the block through safe code, and still violates
what the `unsafe` relies on. Contracts are judged by the side of the boundary they serve:
the gateways through which C reaches the crate, its `ffi_export` regions, and every other
unsafe code, which in a Crustify-generated crate sits in its `ffi_import` regions, whose
items are sound for every input their module can give them, as
[`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section requires.

UB in the workset's API that its UB tests missed, by where it is reached from: the safe

export within the C declaration's contract. The unsafe surface includes only the API the

### 3.4 Equivalence (`equiv`)

Functional equivalence defects in the workset's API that its equivalence tests missed,
while the C it translates exists: in a port, until the module's switch. A divergence is a defect only when it is unintended: a doc comment, a `CHANGELOG`
entry, a named test asserting the new behaviour or a commit message explaining it marks it
deliberate, and one that corrects a C defect on purpose is no finding.

### 3.5 Logic (`logic`)

Behaviour that departs from the library's intended specification, in the workset's public

most authoritative: the formats and standards the library implements, its documentation,

the behaviour departs from. Where the C departs from it too, the defect is not copied into

departs from nearly every specification.

### 3.6 Ergonomics (`ergonomics`)

Public API that is harder to use than it needs to be: its names, its conversions, its
iterators, builders or defaults where the C takes long argument lists, and the standard
traits its types lack. An item's safe API is fixed by the first batch that gives it one, a
wrap included, so its ergonomics are reviewed there.

### 3.7 Idiom (`idiom`)

Ported implementation that transliterates its C rather than using Rust's own means: index
loops where iterators fit, status codes where `Result` and `?` fit, lengths and releases
carried by hand where ownership carries them.

### 3.8 Conventions (`conventions`)

Deviations from the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md), in a Crustify-generated
batch only, unsafe code outside its regions included.

### 3.9 Misc (`misc`)

Any other defect in the workset.

### 3.10 Test adequacy (`test-adequacy`)

Gaps in the workset's tests: the C and Rust execution paths, and the states and
transitions, that the codebase's external and inline test suites leave unreached, found by
reading those suites against the code and measured as
[`testing-builds`](../testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section describes; assertions too
weak to fail when the code is wrong; tests outside the suite of their kind; and the C test
cases none carries over. A gap is filled with tests, not filed: the coverage measurement
shows the delta.

### 3.11 Revisit (`revisit`)

The reports an earlier review filed, each rerun through its reproducer on the current
tree. One that still reproduces stays a finding of its objective; one that no longer does
has its report updated with the commit that changed the verdict; one that was never a
defect is removed, with the reason in the commit message.

### 3.12 Disclosure (`disclose`)

A `disclosure.md` beside each report that the user can send to the affected project's
maintainers unchanged: under 450 words, following the project's conventions for
disclosing security and UB issues, in an email-friendly format naming the maintainers when
it goes by email first. It includes a small snippet and the sanitizer crash or failing
assertion, offers the reproducer on request, and offers patches only under `fix`. It ends
with: `Found by [Crustify](https://github.com/crustify-rs/crustify), an experimental
UB/soundness auditing agent developed at UC Berkeley and running on <model name>, then
manually reviewed and independently reproduced.`

### 3.13 Fix (`fix`)

Whether a review patches what it finds. Without it, a review changes nothing outside
its reviews dir but the tests that fill the gaps `test-adequacy` finds.

## 4. Reports

A review batch files its findings under its reviews dir, as

reproducer, in the sub-directory of its objective:

| objective | sub-directory |
|---|---|
| `unsafety` | `unsafe/` |
| `contracts`, of a gateway | `contracts/ffi_export/` |
| `contracts`, of other unsafe code | `contracts/ffi_import/` |
| `ub`, on the safe interface | `ub_safe/` |
| `ub`, on the unsafe interface | `ub_unsafe/` |

| `ergonomics` | `ergonomics/` |

content.content: --- name: binding description: "How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding: the safe boundary every binding keeps, and the routes binding-types and binding-symbols give types and symbols. Read before binding any item, and when reviewing bindings." --- # Generating safe bindings How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding. A binding keeps the C implementation and puts a safe Rust API in front of it, shaped by the item's analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes. A type takes the type route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md) describes; a symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, macros and lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes. ## 1. Safe boundary Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned. Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to: - wrapped-layout projection; - wrapped FFI calls; and - operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types. They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone: each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the public ones whose obligation no type expresses. A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as [`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so, while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s Equivalence tests section describes. A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names, ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it ports. Every unsafe block carries the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies. An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust, or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the library's bindings wherever that state is shared with C: a lock, a handle or an allocation the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not hold, and reports which in its final message, as [`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw bindings. --- name: binding-types description: "How a scheduled C type becomes a safe Rust binding, binding's type route: its surface, safe layout, lifecycle and field accessors, unions as tagged enums, enums and typedefs. Read before binding any type, and when reviewing bindings." --- # Binding types How a scheduled C type becomes a safe Rust binding: the type route, which follows [`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section; the symbols it reaches are [`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s. [`porting-types`](../../porting/types/SKILL.md) starts from it. ## 1. Surface A binding's surface is the fields and lifecycle primitives the public API publishes: in a wrap batch that precedes its consumers, the fields those consumers access and the type's lifecycle primitives, so that a type none of whose fields they access is bound opaque. Releasers, field disposers, cloners, constructors, casts and pointer-field semantics are identified before a representation is chosen. ## 2. Safe layout A type is bound as a safe layout over the raw type and its handles. The canonical wrapped surface has three types, named as the conventions describe: | type | role | |---|---| | `Foo` | layout-compatible newtype named in every owner and handle, and held by value only in Rust-owned storage (a local, or embedded) | | `FooRef<'a>` | copyable shared borrowed handle with getters | | `FooMut<'a>` | exclusive borrowed handle with setters, and shared and exclusive reborrows | Its owners, which [Lifecycle](#3-lifecycle) describes, are named `FooBox` and `FooArc`, as the conventions name them too. These names are what consumers use, whatever they name: here pointer wrappers and owners over C's allocator, which a port changes, stage by stage, into native borrows and owners, as [`porting-types`](../../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes, without changing its consumers. A consumer relies only on what every form they may take offers: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the native forms offer, which the pointer wrappers mirror. What one form offers beyond that, such as an owner's raw access, is no part of the safe API. No Rust reference to the wrapped C object is ever formed. Borrowed handles contain pointers and carry lifetimes; references to handles cover Rust-owned handle storage only. Layout access starts from `FooRef::as_ptr()` or `FooMut::as_mut_ptr()`, in small justified unsafe blocks. A synthetic type generator is bound as: - a generic wrapper for a homogeneous family converging on the generator; - an alias of a dominant concrete instance to the generator with its element wrapper; and - specializations only for behaviour that differs from the generic surface. ## 3. Lifecycle Every ownership variant the analysis supports has a representation. Owners never dereference to `Foo`; they hand out handles. A sole owner, or a `Foo` value, produces `FooRef` and `FooMut` through `as_ref()` and `as_mut()`. A shared owner without a lock produces `FooRef` directly, and `FooMut` only when it can prove its reference is the only one, or after copying the object. A shared owner whose object carries its own lock produces both through read and write guards, which hold the lock while the handle lives. Lifecycle and clone strategies are stateless, layout-compatible and statically selected when the state is recoverable from the object; runtime state is carried only when construction, destruction or cloning needs external data. A type's constructor and init routines are bound with its lifecycle policy, so that where possible it is exported as a safe function returning the fully-formed object. Every type an argument names is wrapped before it, since a wrap brings in its signature's types. C lifecycle primitives are kept while C can allocate or free the storage. A type whose address C keeps beyond the call that receives it, to read it, call back with it or free it, as the analysis establishes, is never moved while C keeps it: a value of it held by value is never handed to C to keep, and an owner that could move it out is pinned. Promoting construction-phase storage into an owner is unsafe, so it is encapsulated in the type's safe constructor: consumers of the public API never call `assume_init` in their own unsafe blocks. Lifecycle routines are also scheduled as free symbols, although the type route emits them as it binds their types; the symbol route, [`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s, skips those a type batch already emitted. ## 4. Field accessors Each accessor follows from the ownership, mutability, nullability, cardinality and lifetime findings, and every pointer-derived result is tied to the state that keeps it alive. Getters that read `Foo`'s fields are methods in `impl FooRef` blocks taking `&self`, and setters that write them are methods in `impl FooMut` blocks taking `&mut self`. A field is read through the shared handle's pointer and written through the mutable handle's pointer, projected with `addr_of!`, `addr_of_mut!`, `&raw const` or `&raw mut`, never with `&(*p).field` or `&mut (*p).field`. # ffibox

Generic smart pointers and traits for building safe Rust wrappers over C
types and pointers, in both directions: memory C owns, held from Rust, and
memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Designed for arbitrary
user-space C interop, including the case where you need direct field access
and a C-ABI-compatible layout (porting C internals to Rust in place), not just
opaque-handle wrapping.

## Why

Wrapping a C API in Rust means re-homing C's ownership and lifecycle
conventions into RAII. The recurring shapes:

- A C-allocated object with a destructor (`free`), and maybe a copy (`dup`).
- A constructor or allocator (`foo_alloc`, `malloc`, `calloc`) whose result
  must be released by its paired free.
- A refcounted object shared by several holders (`up_ref` / `unref`), maybe
  with a C lock over the state they mutate.
- Types with multiple or runtime-conditional destructors.
- A by-value struct whose teardown disposes its fields but not the struct.
- An owned length-aware buffer or NUL-terminated `char *` with a C destructor.
- A type-erased `void *` that stays opaque end to end.

Each shape gets one owner type, generic over a **policy** — a type you declare
that names the C routines. `impl_cdrop!` and its siblings bind a C routine to a
policy; a type alias names the pair: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`.

## Mental model in one paragraph

No reference to C-owned memory is formed while anything may write or free it:
objects are reached through handles, and only a run of bytes nothing writes
while it is lent is a `&CStr` or `&[u8]`. Each C type gets a layout type
`Foo` (`#[repr(transparent)]` over `ffi::foo`; `Foo<'r>` when the C object
borrows its parent) and two borrowed handles, `FooRef<'a>` / `FooMut<'a>`,
each one pointer wide and carrying the getters and setters; field access projects a raw pointer out of the handle. Ownership
comes in three shapes: `CBox<Foo, P>` is the sole owner of an object behind a
pointer and releases it through the policy `P`; `CArc<Foo, P>` is one of
several counted references and hands out the shared handle, the exclusive one
only when the count proves it sole, and — for an object with a C lock — a
`CGuard` whose `FooLocked<'a>` handle reaches the state that lock protects; and
`CVal<Foo, P>` holds the object inline and disposes its resources on drop.
A policy that also constructs gives `CBox` and `CArc` safe constructors that
allocate through it, so a safely built owner is always freed by the routine
paired with its allocator.
Strings, buffers and borrowed runs get their own types; a buffer drops its
elements, so a `foo **` of owned objects releases each one.

The other direction uses the same terms. `RustAlloc` is the policy over Rust's
allocator, so an object Rust allocates is held as one C allocated, and
`CAllocator` is a C allocation family as the standard `Allocator`, so a
`Box` or `Vec` holds memory C frees; `CClosure`
and `CPayload` put a Rust closure behind a C function pointer and its
context, for one call or until C releases it; `CFn` and `CFnBox` hold a C
function and its context that Rust calls, and `CCallback` and `CCallbackBox`
either half; `CTable` holds Rust state behind a C table of function
pointers C calls into, its slots minted by `impl_cvtable!` from a trait the
Rust side implements; the `export_*!` macros offer a policy to C as the
routine it calls, with the owner and handle types in its signature.
[docs/ownership.md](docs/ownership.md) lists the owners and the policies;
[docs/borrows.md](docs/borrows.md) lists the handles. Each walks from a C
declaration to the type it wants.

## Install

```toml
[dependencies]
ffibox = "0.1"
```

ffibox needs Rust 1.100 or later (`rust-version` in `Cargo.toml`), the first
release with the standard `Allocator` interface, which `CAllocator` implements
over a C allocation family.

ffibox is `#![no_std]`. The `std` feature (on by default) selects
`std::process::abort` for the unrecoverable-failure path (`Clone` or
`make_mut` when the C copy or up_ref fails), where without it that path is a
double-panic, and lets `CClosure`, `CTable`'s slots and `callback::barrier`
catch a panic before it reaches C. The `alloc` feature, which `std` enables,
adds `RustAlloc`, `CPayload`, `CCallbackBox` and `CTable`, which allocate
through Rust's global allocator, and the conversions between ffibox's owners
and `Box` / `Vec`; nothing else allocates but through a policy the consumer
chose, as `CAllocator` allocates through its family.

```toml
[dependencies]
ffibox = { version = "0.1", default-features = false }
```

## Documentation

Every wrapper answers one question first: **does dropping the Rust value
release the object?** This is about who *releases* the object, not who
allocated it — a `CBox` usually points at memory C allocated.

- **Yes** — it is owned → [docs/ownership.md](docs/ownership.md)
- **No** — C, or a parent object, releases it → [docs/borrows.md](docs/borrows.md)

When it is Rust's memory that C holds, calls or reads →
[docs/outbound.md](docs/outbound.md).

| doc | what is in it |
|-----|---------------|
| [goals.md](docs/goals.md) | what the primitives aim for, in both directions, and how each aim is checked |
| [examples.md](docs/examples.md) | eight self-contained wrappers, each compiled as a doctest |
| [ownership.md](docs/ownership.md) | `CBox`, `CBoxState`, `CVal`, `CStrBox`, `CVec`, `CArc`; the lifecycle policies; picking an owner and a policy; `Box` and `Vec` over a C allocator (`CAllocator`) |
| [borrows.md](docs/borrows.md) | `Foo`, `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooLocked`, `CGuard`, `CGuardedRef`, `CSlice`, `CSliceMut`, `CNullTerminated`; where the accessors live; the seam traits |
| [outbound.md](docs/outbound.md) | Rust's side: `RustAlloc`, the callbacks (`CClosure`, `CPayload`, `CFn`, `CFnBox`, `CCallback`, `CCallbackBox`), C tables (`CTable`), out-parameters, the panic barrier, the `export_*!` macros |
| [vtables.md](docs/vtables.md) | C tables of function pointers implemented in Rust: `CTable`, `impl_cvtable!`, their receivers, re-entry, panics and release, and the design |
| [patterns.md](docs/patterns.md) | C's iteration, error and callback conventions as Rust's iterators, `Result` and closures |
| [hand-written.md](docs/hand-written.md) | the wrappers `define_ctype!` cannot express (a layout type generic over a type), and the owners no policy expresses |

Upgrading? [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) says what each release changes, and
how to migrate code that still compiles but behaves differently.

# Goals

ffibox is one vocabulary for every value that crosses the boundary between
Rust and a foreign language, in both directions: memory the foreign side
allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust (**inbound**),
and memory Rust owns that the foreign side holds, calls or reads
(**outbound**). The foreign language is C, as G8 states.

Two parties use each primitive:

- a **producer** implements its unsafe internals: a policy, a layout type, a
  seam, an export. A producer may be a human, an agent or a static analysis
  tool;
- a **consumer** uses it through its safe API, without knowing whether C or
  Rust sits behind it.

ffibox is needed only where the foreign side **aliases** a value: keeps a
pointer to it beyond a call, frees it, or shares its refcount or lock. A
pointer passed down for the duration of one call, and memory the foreign side
never sees, are plain Rust: `&mut`, `&`, `Box`, `Vec`, `Arc`.

The goals below are grouped by what they serve. Each states what it means and
how it is checked.

## Familiarity

### G1. Mirror standard Rust

Each primitive mirrors a standard Rust one a Rust programmer already knows:
`CBox` is `Box`, `CArc` is `Arc`, `CVec` is `Vec`, `CGuard` is `MutexGuard`,
`FooRef` / `FooMut` are `&` / `&mut`. Where a foreign convention has no
standard counterpart, it is expressed as the closest composition of standard
idioms rather than a new concept: a lock over part of an object is `Arc<T>`
with a `Mutex` field; a refcount that proves sole ownership is
`Arc::get_mut`.

Where ownership allows it, each primitive converts to and from its standard
counterpart (`Box`, `Vec`, `Arc`, `CStr`, `&[T]`) and implements the standard
traits its counterpart does (`Clone`, `Debug`, `Iterator`, `Eq`, `Hash`), so
that a consumer can leave ffibox as soon as the foreign side stops aliasing.

*Checked by:* every primitive names its standard counterpart in its
documentation, and every departure from it states why.

### G2. No more discipline than standard Rust

A consumer needs no more care with a primitive than with its standard
counterpart: no ordering rules, no manual release, no invariants to remember.
In particular, a consumer writes no `unsafe`.

*Checked by:* consumer code, and the tests of the safe interface, compile with
`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

### G3. Continue ffibox's style

New primitives continue the style ffibox has established: its terms (owner,
handle, policy, seam, adopt, surrender), its naming patterns (`C`-prefixed
owners, `Foo` / `FooRef` / `FooMut` per type, `impl_*!` per policy trait) and
its preference for reusing one primitive across cases over adding one per
case. This is a direction, not a freeze: a new term, name or primitive is
welcome where it is clearer than stretching an existing one, and it states
what it adds and how it relates to the terms beside it.

*Checked by:* the documentation's walk from a foreign declaration to its
wrapper stays a short decision table per direction, and each term it uses is
defined once.

## Expressiveness

### G4. Ownership conventions as Rust idioms

A foreign language's ownership conventions are expressed with Rust's own:
`Drop` for release, `Clone` for copies and reference counts, lifetimes for
borrows and keepalive, `&` / `&mut` exclusivity for access, `Send` / `Sync`
for thread affinity, `Pin` for address sensitivity, `Option` for nullability
and slices for cardinality. A convention that one primitive cannot express is
a gap in the vocabulary, not a reason for a raw pointer in the consumer's API.

*Checked by:* the public interface of a binding carries no raw pointer and no
`unsafe fn` except where an obligation cannot be expressed in types, each
such case documented.

### G5. Foreign patterns as Rust patterns

Beyond ownership, a foreign API follows recurring patterns, and each is
expressed as the standard Rust trait or idiom it corresponds to, declared in
the foreign language's own terms: the producer names the foreign routines and
conventions, and the primitive supplies the Rust side.

| foreign pattern | Rust pattern |
|-----------------|--------------|
| a cursor advanced by `next(it)` until NULL or a status; a `count` and `get(i)` pair; a `->next` chain; a sentinel-terminated array | `Iterator`, `IntoIterator`, slices |
| a `foreach(callback, context)` visitor | a closure, or an `Iterator` where the visit can be suspended |
| a status code, `errno`, an error out-parameter | `Result` with a typed error |
| out-parameters | return values |
| a read or write callback pair over a stream | `Read`, `Write`, `Seek` |
| a key-value option setter, a configuration struct filled before use | a builder |
| a struct of function pointers a library calls into | a trait the Rust side implements |

A pattern is one primitive, parameterised by the routines that implement it,
so that every API using it reads the same in Rust. In the outbound direction,
the same primitive offers a Rust iterator, error or trait to the foreign side
in its own convention.

*Checked by:* the public interface of a binding exposes no foreign pattern
whose Rust counterpart exists: no cursor to advance by hand, no status code to
check, no out-parameter to fill.

### G6. Both directions, symmetrically

Every primitive serves both directions with the same terms. Adopting has
surrendering; a policy that binds a foreign routine has an export that offers
a Rust routine to the foreign side; a foreign callback has a Rust closure
behind a foreign function pointer; a foreign global has a Rust static the
foreign side reads. Either side can produce any ownership shape, and either
can consume it.

*Checked by:* every inbound primitive names its outbound counterpart, or
states why it has none.

### G7. Composable axes

Shape (one object, a run, a string), policy (what release, copy and
construction mean), sharing (sole or counted), lock scope, thread affinity,
address sensitivity and element ownership are independent axes. Primitives
compose along them: owners are elements of vectors, fields of
`#[repr(C)]` structs and contents of guards, with no primitive of their own
for each combination.

*Checked by:* a new combination of axes needs no new primitive.

### G8. C first

ffibox targets C. Its names, the `C`-prefixed owners, `c_drop`, `as_c_ptr`,
are C's, and so are the conventions its primitives encode: `malloc` and
`free`, refcounts, C locks, NUL-terminated strings, status codes and `errno`,
callbacks with a context pointer. No primitive is shaped for a language ffibox
does not serve yet: C++'s move constructors, exceptions and smart pointers,
and Go's pointer-passing rules, are out of scope for now.

When another language is taken on, its conventions are added beside C's
rather than folded into them, and what the two share is factored out then,
from what they actually share, without changing what C bindings write.

*Checked by:* every primitive serves a convention a C API uses.

## Safety

### G9. UB hazards excluded by construction

A binding built from the primitives cannot reach undefined behaviour from safe
code. Each hazard is excluded by a primitive or a producer's contract:

| hazard | excluded by |
|--------|-------------|
| aliasing a foreign object through a reference | handles: no Rust reference over foreign memory that anything may write or free while the reference lives (C, another handle, another thread), and no `&mut` over memory anything else may access |
| moving an address-sensitive object | pinned owners; inline values only for movable layouts |
| null dereference | `NonNull`, `Option` with the null niche |
| invalid values (`_Bool`, `char`, out-of-range enums) | plain-element markers, open enums |
| reading uninitialised memory | `MaybeUninit`, construction phases, `assume_init` |
| misalignment | layout types, alignment bounds on copies |
| out-of-bounds access | slices and runs carrying their length |
| type confusion through erased pointers | typed erasure and recovery |
| use after free, outliving a keepalive | lifetimes, counted references |
| double release, release by the wrong routine | policies pairing release with allocation |
| data races | `Send` / `Sync` opt-in, lock scopes |
| re-entrancy through callbacks | callback arguments typed by the access the caller holds |
| unwinding or `longjmp` across the boundary | panic barriers, documented non-local exits |

Leaks are not undefined behaviour and are not excluded, but no primitive leaks
except by an explicit surrender.

*Checked by:* each hazard has a test that the binding's safe interface cannot
reach it, a compile-fail test where the type system rejects it.

### G10. Safe by default

Every default is the conservative one: foreign types are neither `Send` nor
`Sync`, adopting a pointer is `unsafe`, no status code is discarded, and an
unknown fact selects the more restrictive primitive. Every relaxation is an
explicit opt-in that states its justification.

*Checked by:* a binding with no opt-ins is sound, if less capable.

### G11. Failure semantics

No panic crosses into the foreign language: exports and callbacks have a
barrier that maps a panic to the routine's error convention. No foreign unwind
or `longjmp` crosses Rust frames with destructors. Allocation failure is a
value, `Option` or `Result`, never an abort. Teardown that fails or panics
still releases each object exactly once.

*Checked by:* tests that panic in callbacks, exports and drops, under the
sanitizers.

### G12. Unsafe encapsulated, obligations local

`unsafe` stays with producers, in policy implementations, layout types, seams
and exports, and is crate-private to the binding wherever it can be. Every
unsafe trait and seam states a falsifiable `# Safety` contract in terms of the
foreign side's observable behaviour, checkable one implementation at a time,
without reasoning about the whole program. The distinct obligations are few
and listed, so that auditing a binding is a checklist.

*Checked by:* every `unsafe impl` and `unsafe` block maps to one listed
obligation.

### G13. Type safety through traits

Generic code is bound by traits rather than raw pointers: a policy implements
the lifecycle traits for the exact type it releases, a routine of the wrong
type does not compile, erased values are recovered through the trait of the
type they hold, and a family of foreign types generated from one template or
macro shares one generic wrapper.

*Checked by:* compile-fail tests binding a routine, an element or an erased
value to the wrong type.

### G14. A small, verified trusted base

ffibox's own unsafe code is minimal, and exercised under Miri with strict
provenance, the sanitizers and BorrowSanitizer. Each misuse it claims to
prevent has a compile-fail test. Its guarantees are only as strong as this
base.

*Checked by:* the test suite runs clean under each instrument.

## Cost

### G15. Zero overhead

A primitive costs what the equivalent raw code costs. With a stateless policy
an owner is pointer-sized and a handle is one pointer; runtime state is
carried only when the foreign contract needs it, and no check is made that the
foreign contract does not require.

*Checked by:* compile-time size assertions, and benchmarks against raw calls.

### G16. ABI fidelity

A primitive that stands in for a foreign value has a guaranteed ABI:
`#[repr(transparent)]` where it crosses by value, the null pointer as `None`,
the foreign layout where the foreign side reads its fields.

*Checked by:* compile-time size and alignment assertions against the foreign
layout.

### G17. Stable Rust, `no_std`, no hidden allocation

ffibox builds on stable Rust, with a declared minimum version, and in
`no_std`. It allocates only through a policy or an allocator the consumer
chose. It uses the standard `Allocator` interface where a primitive needs a
non-global allocator. What only nightly Rust can express, such as Rust-defined
variadic functions, is documented as unsupported.

*Checked by:* CI on the minimum supported version, with and without `std`.

## Production

### G18. Producer-agnostic and deterministic

The primitives do not depend on who produces a binding. A binding follows from
facts about each foreign item: ownership and transfer, access, nullability,
cardinality, keepalive, lifecycle role, thread affinity and address
sensitivity. The choice of primitive is a function of those facts, documented
as a table a human reads, an agent follows and a tool implements. A
fact is visible in the binding's types, so that a reviewer or a tool recovers
the facts from the binding. A fact no producer has established selects the
conservative primitive, as G10 describes, so that a partial analysis still
yields a sound binding, and establishing the fact later relaxes it.

*Checked by:* two producers given the same facts emit the same binding.

### G19. Stable through migration

A consumer's code does not change when the producer behind a primitive
changes: a C allocator replaced by Rust's, a C implementation by a Rust
port. Only the policy changes. This is what lets a codebase be ported one module at a time.

*Checked by:* a ported module's consumers compile unchanged against the port.

### G20. Simple macros

Macros mint only what traits and generics cannot: layout types, handles, and
the impls that name a foreign routine. Everything else is ordinary generic
code, provided methods and blanket impls, which the compiler checks and
documents. Each macro does one thing, with a few arms that differ only in
optional trailing parameters; a variant whose expansion differs is a macro of
its own with its own name, as `impl_cdrop_str!` is beside `impl_cdrop!`,
rather than another arm of a larger one. A misuse fails with a type error at
the invocation, not inside the expansion.

*Checked by:* each macro's expansion reads as the impl a producer would write
by hand, and fits on a screen.

## Non-goals

- **Finding the facts.** ffibox records ownership facts in types; it does not
  infer them. Inference is the producer's: a human, an agent or an analysis.
- **Generating bindings.** ffibox is what bindings are written in, not a
  generator. Its regularity serves generators.
- **Memory the foreign side does not alias.** That is standard Rust's.
- **Foreign languages other than C, for now.** See G8.

# Goals

ffibox is one vocabulary for every value that crosses the boundary between
Rust and a foreign language, in both directions: memory the foreign side
allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust (**inbound**),
and memory Rust owns that the foreign side holds, calls or reads
(**outbound**). The foreign language is C, as G8 states.

Two parties use each primitive:

- a **producer** implements its unsafe internals: a policy, a layout type, a
  seam, an export. A producer may be a human, an agent or a static analysis
  tool;
- a **consumer** uses it through its safe API, without knowing whether C or
  Rust sits behind it.

ffibox is needed only where the foreign side **aliases** a value: keeps a
pointer to it beyond a call, frees it, or shares its refcount or lock. A
pointer passed down for the duration of one call, and memory the foreign side
never sees, are plain Rust: `&mut`, `&`, `Box`, `Vec`, `Arc`.

The goals below are grouped by what they serve. Each states what it means and
how it is checked.

## Familiarity

### G1. Mirror standard Rust

Each primitive mirrors a standard Rust one a Rust programmer already knows:
`CBox` is `Box`, `CArc` is `Arc`, `CVec` is `Vec`, `CGuard` is `MutexGuard`,
`FooRef` / `FooMut` are `&` / `&mut`. Where a foreign convention has no
standard counterpart, it is expressed as the closest composition of standard
idioms rather than a new concept: a lock over part of an object is `Arc<T>`
with a `Mutex` field; a refcount that proves sole ownership is
`Arc::get_mut`.

Where ownership allows it, each primitive converts to and from its standard
counterpart (`Box`, `Vec`, `Arc`, `CStr`, `&[T]`) and implements the standard
traits its counterpart does (`Clone`, `Debug`, `Iterator`, `Eq`, `Hash`), so
that a consumer can leave ffibox as soon as the foreign side stops aliasing.

*Checked by:* every primitive names its standard counterpart in its
documentation, and every departure from it states why.

### G2. No more discipline than standard Rust

A consumer needs no more care with a primitive than with its standard
counterpart: no ordering rules, no manual release, no invariants to remember.
In particular, a consumer writes no `unsafe`.

*Checked by:* consumer code, and the tests of the safe interface, compile with
`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

### G3. Continue ffibox's style

New primitives continue the style ffibox has established: its terms (owner,
handle, policy, seam, adopt, surrender), its naming patterns (`C`-prefixed
owners, `Foo` / `FooRef` / `FooMut` per type, `impl_*!` per policy trait) and
its preference for reusing one primitive across cases over adding one per
case. This is a direction, not a freeze: a new term, name or primitive is
welcome where it is clearer than stretching an existing one, and it states
what it adds and how it relates to the terms beside it.

*Checked by:* the documentation's walk from a foreign declaration to its
wrapper stays a short decision table per direction, and each term it uses is
defined once.

## Expressiveness

### G4. Ownership conventions as Rust idioms

A foreign language's ownership conventions are expressed with Rust's own:
`Drop` for release, `Clone` for copies and reference counts, lifetimes for
borrows and keepalive, `&` / `&mut` exclusivity for access, `Send` / `Sync`
for thread affinity, `Pin` for address sensitivity, `Option` for nullability
and slices for cardinality. A convention that one primitive cannot express is
a gap in the vocabulary, not a reason for a raw pointer in the consumer's API.

*Checked by:* the public interface of a binding carries no raw pointer and no
`unsafe fn` except where an obligation cannot be expressed in types, each
such case documented.

### G5. Foreign patterns as Rust patterns

Beyond ownership, a foreign API follows recurring patterns, and each is
expressed as the standard Rust trait or idiom it corresponds to, declared in
the foreign language's own terms: the producer names the foreign routines and
conventions, and the primitive supplies the Rust side.

| foreign pattern | Rust pattern |
|-----------------|--------------|
| a cursor advanced by `next(it)` until NULL or a status; a `count` and `get(i)` pair; a `->next` chain; a sentinel-terminated array | `Iterator`, `IntoIterator`, slices |
| a `foreach(callback, context)` visitor | a closure, or an `Iterator` where the visit can be suspended |
| a status code, `errno`, an error out-parameter | `Result` with a typed error |
| out-parameters | return values |
| a read or write callback pair over a stream | `Read`, `Write`, `Seek` |
| a key-value option setter, a configuration struct filled before use | a builder |
| a struct of function pointers a library calls into | a trait the Rust side implements |

A pattern is one primitive, parameterised by the routines that implement it,
so that every API using it reads the same in Rust. In the outbound direction,
the same primitive offers a Rust iterator, error or trait to the foreign side
in its own convention.

*Checked by:* the public interface of a binding exposes no foreign pattern
whose Rust counterpart exists: no cursor to advance by hand, no status code to
check, no out-parameter to fill.

### G6. Both directions, symmetrically

Every primitive serves both directions with the same terms. Adopting has
surrendering; a policy that binds a foreign routine has an export that offers
a Rust routine to the foreign side; a foreign callback has a Rust closure
behind a foreign function pointer; a foreign global has a Rust static the
foreign side reads. Either side can produce any ownership shape, and either
can consume it.

*Checked by:* every inbound primitive names its outbound counterpart, or
states why it has none.

### G7. Composable axes

Shape (one object, a run, a string), policy (what release, copy and
construction mean), sharing (sole or counted), lock scope, thread affinity,
address sensitivity and element ownership are independent axes. Primitives
compose along them: owners are elements of vectors, fields of
`#[repr(C)]` structs and contents of guards, with no primitive of their own
for each combination.

*Checked by:* a new combination of axes needs no new primitive.

### G8. C first

ffibox targets C. Its names, the `C`-prefixed owners, `c_drop`, `as_c_ptr`,
are C's, and so are the conventions its primitives encode: `malloc` and
`free`, refcounts, C locks, NUL-terminated strings, status codes and `errno`,
callbacks with a context pointer. No primitive is shaped for a language ffibox
does not serve yet: C++'s move constructors, exceptions and smart pointers,
and Go's pointer-passing rules, are out of scope for now.

When another language is taken on, its conventions are added beside C's
rather than folded into them, and what the two share is factored out then,
from what they actually share, without changing what C bindings write.

*Checked by:* every primitive serves a convention a C API uses.

## Safety

### G9. UB hazards excluded by construction

A binding built from the primitives cannot reach undefined behaviour from safe
code. Each hazard is excluded by a primitive or a producer's contract:

| hazard | excluded by |
|--------|-------------|
| aliasing a foreign object through a reference | handles: no Rust reference over foreign memory that anything may write or free while the reference lives (C, another handle, another thread), and no `&mut` over memory anything else may access |
| moving an address-sensitive object | pinned owners; inline values only for movable layouts |
| null dereference | `NonNull`, `Option` with the null niche |
| invalid values (`_Bool`, `char`, out-of-range enums) | plain-element markers, open enums |
| reading uninitialised memory | `MaybeUninit`, construction phases, `assume_init` |
| misalignment | layout types, alignment bounds on copies |
| out-of-bounds access | slices and runs carrying their length |
| type confusion through erased pointers | typed erasure and recovery |
| use after free, outliving a keepalive | lifetimes, counted references |
| double release, release by the wrong routine | policies pairing release with allocation |
| data races | `Send` / `Sync` opt-in, lock scopes |
| re-entrancy through callbacks | callback arguments typed by the access the caller holds |
| unwinding or `longjmp` across the boundary | panic barriers, documented non-local exits |

Leaks are not undefined behaviour and are not excluded, but no primitive leaks
except by an explicit surrender.

*Checked by:* each hazard has a test that the binding's safe interface cannot
reach it, a compile-fail test where the type system rejects it.

### G10. Safe by default

Every default is the conservative one: foreign types are neither `Send` nor
`Sync`, adopting a pointer is `unsafe`, no status code is discarded, and an
unknown fact selects the more restrictive primitive. Every relaxation is an
explicit opt-in that states its justification.

*Checked by:* a binding with no opt-ins is sound, if less capable.

### G11. Failure semantics

No panic crosses into the foreign language: exports and callbacks have a
barrier that maps a panic to the routine's error convention. No foreign unwind
or `longjmp` crosses Rust frames with destructors. Allocation failure is a
value, `Option` or `Result`, never an abort. Teardown that fails or panics
still releases each object exactly once.

*Checked by:* tests that panic in callbacks, exports and drops, under the
sanitizers.

### G12. Unsafe encapsulated, obligations local

`unsafe` stays with producers, in policy implementations, layout types, seams
and exports, and is crate-private to the binding wherever it can be. Every
unsafe trait and seam states a falsifiable `# Safety` contract in terms of the
foreign side's observable behaviour, checkable one implementation at a time,
without reasoning about the whole program. The distinct obligations are few
and listed, so that auditing a binding is a checklist.

*Checked by:* every `unsafe impl` and `unsafe` block maps to one listed
obligation.

### G13. Type safety through traits

Generic code is bound by traits rather than raw pointers: a policy implements
the lifecycle traits for the exact type it releases, a routine of the wrong
type does not compile, erased values are recovered through the trait of the
type they hold, and a family of foreign types generated from one template or
macro shares one generic wrapper.

*Checked by:* compile-fail tests binding a routine, an element or an erased
value to the wrong type.

### G14. A small, verified trusted base

ffibox's own unsafe code is minimal, and exercised under Miri with strict
provenance, the sanitizers and BorrowSanitizer. Each misuse it claims to
prevent has a compile-fail test. Its guarantees are only as strong as this
base.

*Checked by:* the test suite runs clean under each instrument.

## Cost

### G15. Zero overhead

A primitive costs what the equivalent raw code costs. With a stateless policy
an owner is pointer-sized and a handle is one pointer; runtime state is
carried only when the foreign contract needs it, and no check is made that the
foreign contract does not require.

*Checked by:* compile-time size assertions, and benchmarks against raw calls.

### G16. ABI fidelity

A primitive that stands in for a foreign value has a guaranteed ABI:
`#[repr(transparent)]` where it crosses by value, the null pointer as `None`,
the foreign layout where the foreign side reads its fields.

*Checked by:* compile-time size and alignment assertions against the foreign
layout.

### G17. Stable Rust, `no_std`, no hidden allocation

ffibox builds on stable Rust, with a declared minimum version, and in
`no_std`. It allocates only through a policy or an allocator the consumer
chose. It uses the standard `Allocator` interface where a primitive needs a
non-global allocator. What only nightly Rust can express, such as Rust-defined
variadic functions, is documented as unsupported.

*Checked by:* CI on the minimum supported version, with and without `std`.

## Production

### G18. Producer-agnostic and deterministic

The primitives do not depend on who produces a binding. A binding follows from
facts about each foreign item: ownership and transfer, access, nullability,
cardinality, keepalive, lifecycle role, thread affinity and address
sensitivity. The choice of primitive is a function of those facts, documented
as a table a human reads, an agent follows and a tool implements. A
fact is visible in the binding's types, so that a reviewer or a tool recovers
the facts from the binding. A fact no producer has established selects the
conservative primitive, as G10 describes, so that a partial analysis still
yields a sound binding, and establishing the fact later relaxes it.

*Checked by:* two producers given the same facts emit the same binding.

### G19. Stable through migration

A consumer's code does not change when the producer behind a primitive
changes: a C allocator replaced by Rust's, a C implementation by a Rust
port. Only the policy changes. This is what lets a codebase be ported one module at a time.

*Checked by:* a ported module's consumers compile unchanged against the port.

### G20. Simple macros

Macros mint only what traits and generics cannot: layout types, handles, and
the impls that name a foreign routine. Everything else is ordinary generic
code, provided methods and blanket impls, which the compiler checks and
documents. Each macro does one thing, with a few arms that differ only in
optional trailing parameters; a variant whose expansion differs is a macro of
its own with its own name, as `impl_cdrop_str!` is beside `impl_cdrop!`,
rather than another arm of a larger one. A misuse fails with a type error at
the invocation, not inside the expansion.

*Checked by:* each macro's expansion reads as the impl a producer would write
by hand, and fits on a screen.

## Non-goals

- **Finding the facts.** ffibox records ownership facts in types; it does not
  infer them. Inference is the producer's: a human, an agent or an analysis.
- **Generating bindings.** ffibox is what bindings are written in, not a
  generator. Its regularity serves generators.
- **Memory the foreign side does not alias.** That is standard Rust's.
- **Foreign languages other than C, for now.** See G8.

# Borrows

A borrow is a handle over an object something else releases — C, or a parent
object. It is one pointer wide, carries a lifetime, and is never a Rust
reference to the C object itself.

For the owning side — values whose drop releases the object — see
[ownership.md](ownership.md).

## The handles

| Scope | Type | From | Role |
|-------|------|------|------|
| per C type | `Foo` | `define_ctype!` | the layout, the C struct's size: `#[repr(transparent)]` over `ffi::foo`, embeds by value in a `#[repr(C)]` mirror, and is what a `CBox` points at. Never referenced over C-owned memory. Also the value itself when it owns no resources (a rational `{ num, den }`). |
| | `FooRef<'a>` | `define_ctype!` | shared borrow, one pointer wide, `Copy`; the getters |
| | `FooMut<'a>` | `define_ctype!` | exclusive borrow, move-only; the setters, and the getters through `as_ref()` |
| per C lock | `FooLocked<'a>` | `impl_cguarded!` | exclusive borrow under the C lock, move-only; getters and setters for the state the lock protects, the unlocked getters through `as_ref()` |
| lock | `CGuard<'a, Foo>` | ffibox | a held C lock, unlocking on drop — `MutexGuard`; `as_locked()` → `FooLocked<'_>`, `as_ref()` → `FooRef<'_>` |
| guarded borrow | `CGuardedRef<'a, Foo>` | ffibox | an object under one lock covering all of it (`CGuardedAll`), never released — typically a C global (`'static`); only `lock()`, whose `as_locked()` is `FooMut` — `&Mutex<_>` |
| views | `CSlice<'a, T>` / `CSliceMut<'a, T>` | ffibox | any borrowed run of elements — a buffer's, a struct field's, a getter's — as handles or copies, never a `&[T]`; only a run of plain values nothing writes while it is lent is a `&[T]` instead, as [Choosing a borrow](#choosing-a-borrow) describes |
| | `CNullTerminated<'a, T>` | ffibox | a NULL-terminated array of pointers (`char **`, `foo **`), iterated as `&CStr`s or `FooRef`s |

A layout type that carries a lifetime, over a C object that keeps a pointer
to its parent, is `define_ctype!`'s too: `define_ctype!(Blob<'r>, BlobRef,
BlobMut, ffi::blob, phantom = &'r Repo)` gives `Blob<'r>`, `BlobRef<'a, 'r>`
and `BlobMut<'a, 'r>`, the marker deciding how `Blob` varies in `'r`. A
wrapper that needs type parameters (derived sub-types over a generic field) is
written by hand against the same contract — see
[Under the hood](hand-written.md). Its policies still come from the macros
where they take the type.

## Conventions

- **Accessors live on the handles.** Getters on `FooRef<'a>` taking `&self`,
  setters on `FooMut<'a>` taking `&mut self`; `FooMut` reaches the getters with
  `as_ref()`, so they are written once. Both project a raw pointer out of the
  handle and read or write through `addr_of!` / `addr_of_mut!`.
- **Every holder reaches the handles the same way:** `as_ref()` / `as_mut()` on
  `Foo`, `CBox`, `CBoxState`, `CVal` and `FooMut` itself (where `as_mut()` is
  the reborrow `&mut` gets implicitly: `helper(m.as_mut())` keeps `m`);
  `as_ref()` on `CArc`, whose exclusive handle comes only from `get_mut()` /
  `make_mut()`; `as_ref()` / `as_locked()` on a `CGuard` and on `FooLocked` (where
  `as_locked()` reborrows). `CSliceMut` reborrows the same
  way, and splits and sub-ranges like `&mut [T]`. Never `Deref`:
  `Deref::Target` cannot name a lifetime taken from `&self`, and since `FooRef`
  is `Copy`, a `Deref<Target = FooRef<'a>>` on `FooMut` would let safe code copy
  a shared handle out while keeping the exclusive one.
- **No reference covers C memory anything may write.** `&FooRef` covers one pointer of Rust stack,
  never the object. The one place a reference covers a C struct's bytes is
  `Foo::as_ref` / `as_mut` on a value Rust holds inline. A run of bytes an
  object lends, a NUL string or a counted run, is lent as `&CStr` or `&[u8]`
  only while nothing writes it, as [Choosing a borrow](#choosing-a-borrow)
  describes; otherwise it is a `CSlice`.
- **The handles' seams are traits the macros implement:** `CRefSeam` on
  `FooRef` (`from_ptr`, `as_ptr` and the `void *` pair), `CMutSeam` on `FooMut`
  (`from_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr` and the `void *` pair) and `CLockedSeam` on
  `FooLocked` (`as_mut_ptr` alone). Import them wherever the seam is used, in
  the crate that invokes `define_ctype!` or in any other that holds its
  handles. Their methods are provided once, by ffibox, so the wrapper crate
  defines no raw-pointer method of its own for them. The inbound half is also
  on `CCell` (`ref_from_ptr`, `mut_from_ptr` and the `void *` twins), so
  generic code over `T: CCell` can borrow a pointer C gives it; those are
  `unsafe`, and the handles' `from_ptr` forward to them. Adopting ownership is
  a different verb on a different type — see
  [ownership.md](ownership.md#conventions).

## Choosing a borrow

Reached when dropping the Rust value does *not* release the object. When it
does, the answer is an owner — see
[ownership.md](ownership.md#choosing-an-owner-what-shape-is-the-owned-thing).

- **No — C, or a parent object, releases it.** Borrow it:
  - one object → `FooRef<'a>` / `FooMut<'a>`, its lifetime tied to whatever
    keeps it alive (a parent's handle, the call);
  - a run of elements → `CSlice<'a, T>` / `CSliceMut<'a, T>`;
  - a counted run of immutable bytes an object lends, `const uint8_t *data`
    with its `size_t len` (from a getter pair, or two fields) → `&'a [u8]`
    from `core::slice::from_raw_parts`, tied to the shared handle's `'a`, as a
    NUL string is a `&CStr`. A run of other `CPlainElem` values is the same
    `&'a [T]`. The SAFETY comment shows, from C's contract, that:
    - nothing writes, moves or frees the bytes while the shared handle lives:
      no routine reachable through a `FooRef` writes, grows or reallocates
      them (not one on `FooRef`, not one on a `FooLocked` taken beside it, not
      another thread's, if `Foo` is `Sync`); a write reachable only through
      `FooMut` is excluded by the borrow;
    - they live as long as the object does, freed with it or with a parent the
      lifetime covers, not by the next call that refills a shared buffer; and
    - `data` addresses `len` initialised bytes in one allocation. A NULL or
      empty run returns `&[]` without the call, since `from_raw_parts` takes
      no NULL even for a length of 0.

    Where any of these fails, as for a cache, a buffer the library refills or
    reallocates behind a `const` pointer, or state another thread writes, the
    run is a `CSlice<'a, u8>` built with `CSlice::from_raw_parts`, which forms
    no reference: `elems`, `copy_to_slice` and `to_cvec` copy the bytes out.
    The element type does not decide between the two, since a `u8` is plain
    either way: who may write the bytes does. A caller that keeps the bytes
    past the object's borrow takes an owned copy;
  - a NULL-terminated array of pointers → `CNullTerminated<'a, T>`, an
    `Iterator` of the elements' borrows; a `count` + `get(i)` pair or a
    `->next` chain is `(0..n).map(get)` or `iter::successors` over the safe
    getter;
  - an object every access reaches under one lock covering all of it —
    typically a C global and the C lock protecting it → `CGuardedRef<'a, Foo>`,
    `'static` for a global, with `impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)`;
  - a NUL string → `&CStr` / `&str` / `&[u8]` tied to the owner's borrow,
    on the terms of a counted byte run above;
  - an out-parameter slot → `&'a mut MaybeUninit<T>` from
    `ptr.cast::<MaybeUninit<T>>().as_mut()`; no ffibox type;
  - a `void *` → if it is really a `ffi::foo`, erase a `FooRef` with
    `as_void_ptr` and recover it with `from_void_ptr` (generically,
    `T::ref_from_void_ptr` / `T::mut_from_void_ptr` for `T: CCell`); if it is a
    cookie never looked inside, pass the raw `*mut c_void` through unchanged.

  A borrow that must outlive its parent's scope (stored next to the parent,
  sent to a thread) cannot be expressed as a lifetime; copy the child into an
  owned object instead.
